one_line_idea: The compute-optimal parameter-to-data balance for vision encoder pretraining sits far from the language-model Chinchilla ratio, and a vision-specific allocation rule fitted from small runs changes how pretraining budgets should be spent.
Input resolution is a third scaling axis with its own exponent, and vision loss is better modeled as L(params, data, resolution) than by folding resolution into compute.

Tokens-per-image, not parameter count, is the dominant scale variable for dense-prediction transfer from ViTs, and parameter scaling at fixed token count buys almost nothing for localization-heavy tasks.

Published vision scaling-law fits are functional-form-degenerate: saturating and pure power-law forms fit the observed range equally well but diverge by large factors at the extrapolation targets used to justify frontier training runs.
The data-scaling exponent of a vision model is set by the Zipf tail of concept frequencies in its pretraining corpus, and reshaping that tail moves the exponent in a predictable direction.

Scaling-curve-based decisions beat endpoint comparisons at equal pilot compute: fitting mini scaling laws over nested data sizes ranks pretraining-data choices for large scale more accurately than comparing single matched runs.

Vision encoders exhibit transfer ossification: pretraining past the data-optimal point on a fixed corpus makes them measurably worse fine-tuning initializations than earlier checkpoints, at every downstream budget.

Parameter scaling and data scaling buy different error components in dense transfer: data buys semantic coverage, parameters buy localization precision, and the two are separable by error taxonomy at matched upstream loss.

Compute-optimal pretraining for transfer is not compute-optimal for upstream loss: optimizing the parameter-data split directly against downstream fine-tuned performance shifts the optimum toward more data and smaller models by a fittable factor.

Task label granularity sets the data-scaling exponent: fine-grained recognition error falls with pretraining data at a systematically steeper exponent than coarse recognition, making granularity a predictor of who benefits from the next data doubling.

Architecture changes the constant, not the exponent: FLOP-matched ConvNet and ViT families pretrained on the same data have statistically indistinguishable scaling exponents, so architecture debates are debates about offsets.

The upstream-downstream correlation breaks at a predictable scale: beyond a threshold, further upstream-loss improvements stop predicting dense-task transfer gains, and the divergence point can be located with cheap probes.

Frozen-probe transfer and fine-tuned transfer scale with different exponents, and the widening gap is a direct measurement of how much task-relevant structure pretraining still fails to expose linearly.

A public dense-transfer scaling atlas: per-task exponents for depth, detection, keypoints, and surface normals against encoder data and model scale, packaged so practitioners can forecast whether the next encoder generation will move their task.

Semantic content scales faster than spatial precision in foundation features: what-information grows with a larger exponent than where-information, quantifying why dense tasks lag classification as encoders scale.

In detection transfer, rare classes ride the data axis and common classes ride the model axis: per-class transfer gains decompose by pretraining-frequency bin, with tail classes gaining almost exclusively from data scale.

A substitution law between pretraining data and downstream labels: each 10x of encoder pretraining data replaces a measurable, task-dependent multiple of labeled fine-tuning examples, enabling label-budget arithmetic.
Small-object detection gains come from resolution, not encoder scale: below a pixel-size floor, encoder scaling has near-zero effect and input-resolution scaling carries the entire improvement.

Reported dense-transfer scaling gains across encoder releases are substantially resolution-schedule artifacts: controlling for training-resolution differences shrinks claimed scale effects by half or more.

Mask-supervised pretraining data (SA-1B-style) scales boundary quality with a better exponent than region agreement: dense-supervision data buys edges, not regions, relative to classification-supervised scaling.

The crossover scale where generic encoder plus light decoder matches specialized end-to-end models is predictable from task output complexity, giving each dense task a forecastable retirement date for bespoke architectures.
Decoder scaling has an exponent near zero once past a small size: in encoder-decoder dense pipelines, virtually all scalable improvement lives in the encoder axis, and decoder growth is dead compute.

A domain-mixture scaling law for real web data: target-domain transfer follows a fittable function of mixture weight and total data, so optimal real-data mixtures at large scale are predictable from small pilot grids.

Text-in-image fraction is the hidden knob behind OCR-adjacent abilities of contrastive vision models: reading-like capabilities track the share of photos containing legible text, with a threshold onset.

Regional data share obeys a saturating law with a cheap equalization frontier: raising under-represented regions' share improves region-specific performance steeply at first, at near-zero cost to head-region performance until a measurable knee.

The object-centric versus scene-centric composition of pretraining photos controls the classification-versus-dense-transfer trade-off, and the currently accidental ratio in web corpora is far from dense-task-optimal.

Effective dataset size is unique-cluster count: transfer performance of web-pretrained encoders is predicted by the number of near-duplicate clusters, not raw image count, unifying corpora of wildly different redundancy under one curve.

Caption specificity distribution of real alt-text is a first-class composition variable: reweighting toward object-naming captions changes zero-shot classification far more than equal-count changes in image content.
Per-concept accuracy follows a near-universal power law in per-concept pretraining count with a shared exponent across concepts, reducing composition design to allocating counts along one curve.

The native-resolution distribution of the pretraining corpus imprints a scale prior on encoders: models systematically underperform at object scales rare in their corpus, and resolution-mix reshaping moves the failure profile predictably.

Concept drift of the visual world is fittable as a per-year decay law: models pretrained on older real crawls lose accuracy on newer-world probes at a measurable rate, giving corpora a quantifiable shelf life.

People-image share has decoupled utility and privacy curves: person-task transfer saturates at a modest share while memorization of individuals keeps rising, so current corpora sit past the utility knee but still on the risk ramp.

Contextual bias is a dose-dependent function of co-occurrence statistics in pretraining data: resampling rare-context images measurably improves out-of-context recognition at a fittable exchange rate.

Composition effects are log-additive: domain-share effects on downstream log-error superpose across domains, so full mixture response surfaces can be predicted from single-domain sweeps and solved by linear algebra.

Vision pretraining tolerates far more data repetition than language lore implies: the per-epoch effective-data decay constant is small under strong augmentation, and the unique-data premium has been overstated for vision.

Augmentation is a data multiplier with a scale-decaying exchange rate: its effective-dataset-size factor is large for small models and shrinks predictably with model scale, so augmentation-heavy recipes are a small-model subsidy.
Targeted repetition beats uniform repetition: oversampling tail-concept images when repeating a fixed corpus recovers a large share of the benefit of new tail data, at zero collection cost.
Epochs buy fit, unique data buys coverage: repetition and fresh data improve dissociable error components, and the decomposition predicts which failure modes more epochs can and cannot fix.

The one-epoch-is-optimal folklore imported from web-scale language training is wrong for vision contrastive learning: the accuracy-optimal repetition count under realistic data constraints is well above one and predictable from corpus size.

Aggressive near-duplicate removal hurts fine-grained recognition: near-duplicates of the same instance are free hard positives, and the dedup-threshold optimum is task-dependent rather than universal.

A collection-versus-repetition stopping rule: fitting the repetition-decay law on pilot runs yields a break-even collection cost per image, telling data-constrained teams exactly when to stop collecting real data and start repeating.

Memorization onset precedes utility loss under repetition: as epochs accumulate there is a window where accuracy still improves while per-image memorization risk is already climbing steeply, so utility-monitored training silently walks into privacy debt.

Wild duplication spectra make web corpora behave far smaller than their headline size: an effective-sample-size formula computed from the duplication histogram predicts transfer as if the corpus were a fraction of its raw count.

Capability onset is set by absolute exemplar count, not scale: injecting a controlled number of capability-relevant real images moves the emergence point of visual capabilities to smaller compute, by a predictable amount.

Behavioral emergence has representational precursors: linear-probe competence for a capability appears roughly an order of magnitude of compute before behavioral competence, enabling an early-warning forecaster for capability arrival.

Emergent object grouping in self-supervised attention is a percolation transition: attention-graph connectivity crosses a threshold as data grows, and object-centric data composition moves the transition point.

Attribute-object binding emerges only when pretraining data decorrelates attributes from objects: binding capability tracks the count of counter-stereotypical pairings, not total data, and can be induced early by decorrelation-targeted resampling.

Emergence abruptness is predicted by task decomposability: capabilities with probeable independent sub-skills scale smoothly, while non-decomposable capabilities show genuinely discontinuous competence growth even under continuous metrics.

Representational geometry reorganizes before capabilities arrive: intrinsic-dimension and cluster-structure shifts in feature space are early-warning signatures that precede capability onsets along scale ladders.

Capabilities emerge in a universal order set by data statistics: onset ordering across capability batteries is nearly identical across architectures trained on the same corpus, and reshuffles when the corpus changes.

Much of what is booked as scale-driven emergence is rare-slice sampling: many capability onsets attributed to model scale are reproducible at 10x smaller compute by reweighting fixed data toward the relevant slice.

Some emergent behaviors are memorization in disguise: capabilities that appear at scale can be retrieval of rare memorized templates, distinguishable from generalization-emergence by near-duplicate-controlled probes.

Deja-vu-style memorization in self-supervised encoders follows a scaling law in model size at fixed data: per-image recoverability grows with a fittable exponent, making privacy risk of future releases forecastable.

Duplication dose-response for discriminative memorization has a sharp knee: per-image membership signal is near-floor below a duplication threshold and rises steeply above it, giving dedup policy a principled operating point.

Which images a vision model will memorize is predictable before training: a risk score from data-level properties alone (duplication, local density, atypicality) identifies most eventually-memorized images without touching the model.

Dense models memorize regions, not images: memorization in detectors and depth networks concentrates on rare object instances within scenes, so region-level audits find leakage that image-level audits miss entirely.

Detectors replay memorized rare instances: context similar to a memorized training scene triggers hallucinated detections of the memorized object, a failure mode invisible to aggregate AP and traceable to duplication.

Memorization decays under fresh data with a fittable forgetting law: scheduling a clean-data tail at the end of pretraining purges most early-acquired memorization at small utility cost, yielding a data-level privacy mitigation.

The marginal capability of the last 10x of encoder scale is disproportionately tail memorization: decomposing scale gains by example typicality shows generalization gains saturating while memorization-like gains keep growing.

Supervised and self-supervised models memorize different things: label-coupled memorization versus content memorization dissociate under attack, and mitigations tuned for one transfer poorly to the other.

Pretraining memorization survives downstream fine-tuning: membership of pretraining images remains detectable from fully fine-tuned dense-task models, so releasing a fine-tuned model leaks the pretraining set.

Memorization dosimetry for vision releases: a standardized panel of real held-out images injected at graded duplication counts turns per-model privacy risk into a measured dose-response curve reportable on model cards.

Augmentation strength buys privacy at a measurable exchange rate: stronger cropping and color jitter suppress per-image memorization with a fittable privacy-utility frontier, and some augmentation regimes are strictly dominant.

Encoders memorize background people: individuals occupying under 5% of image pixels are re-identifiable from embeddings of held-out photos, and selective face/person blurring of the corpus removes the risk at near-zero utility cost.

Membership risk of vision encoders follows a capacity-to-data ratio law: attack AUC across models and corpora collapses onto a single curve in parameters-per-unique-image, giving a one-number risk predictor.

Structured outputs leak more: membership inference against dense predictors using spatially resolved error patterns beats pooled image-level attacks by a wide margin, because per-location residuals carry per-image fingerprints.
Average-case membership metrics hide a vulnerable tail whose size is set by the duplication spectrum: TPR at very low FPR is high for a predictable subset even when aggregate AUC looks safe.

Shadow models are replaceable by data statistics: normalizing attack scores with per-example difficulty estimated from corpus-level features matches shadow-model attacks at a hundredth of the compute, democratizing encoder audits.

Membership signals transfer across models trained on overlapping crawls: an attack fitted on a small open encoder identifies members of a large closed encoder's corpus, because web-crawl overlap makes membership a property of the image, not the model.

Distilled students inherit their teacher's membership secrets: distillation on disjoint transfer data still moves enough per-example signal that the teacher's training members are detectable from the student alone.

Bigger is not leakier at web scale: at fixed unique data, membership risk grows with model size, but along the realistic joint-scaling path (data grows with model) per-image risk falls, inverting the intuitive scale-risk narrative.

Collection-level membership auditing: aggregating weak per-image signals across a photographer's or institution's entire collection yields high-confidence dataset-inclusion tests even when every individual image is undetectable.

Reported membership-inference success on vision foundation models is inflated by member/non-member distribution mismatch: attacks are partly detecting which crawl an image came from, not whether the model saw it.

User-level membership is the real exposure: aggregating over the many photos a person contributes to web corpora makes individuals detectable at rates far beyond per-image analysis, scaling with photos-per-user.
Better encoders are more invertible: input-image reconstructability from frozen patch tokens increases with encoder scale, contradicting the intuition that more abstract features are safer to share.

Global embeddings re-identify: a single CLIP-style image vector suffices to link a person or place across photo collections at rates that make embedding release equivalent to content release for linkage purposes.

Redact-then-encode fails: content masked out of an image before encoding is partially recoverable from the visible-region tokens, because attention mixes neighborhood evidence into every token, and the leak grows with encoder scale.

Dense features are location beacons: mid-layer features of general-purpose encoders support geolocation of ordinary photos far above prior-based baselines, and pretraining data scale drives the effect.

A measured privacy-utility frontier for feature release: quantization, dimension reduction, and token pooling cut inversion and linkage risk at quantified utility costs, yielding a publishable recipe instead of folklore.

The deep-cut-is-safe heuristic of split inference fails slowly: invertibility declines with cut depth only as a shallow power law, so even late-layer features leak reconstructable content, and the curve quantifies exactly how much safety each layer buys.
Black-box extraction from discriminative dense models: querying a deployed depth or detection model with crafted probe images mines memorized training-scene content without any feature access.

Embedding privacy decays over time without anyone touching the data: vectors released today become more linkable every year as public encoder quality improves, so feature releases carry a growing retroactive risk.

Similarity graphs leak the images: releasing only a kNN graph or similarity matrix of a private image collection allows attribute and identity recovery through graph-structure matching against public references.

A contamination inflation law: benchmark-score inflation is a fittable function of duplication count, similarity level, and model scale, turning contamination audits from binary accusations into quantitative score corrections.

Contamination grows a generalization halo with scale: at small scale contaminated items inflate only their own scores, but at larger scale the benefit spreads to related uncontaminated items, blurring the line between cheating and learning.

Unlabeled test images in pretraining are contamination too: self-supervised exposure to benchmark images without labels measurably inflates downstream linear-probe and fine-tuned scores on those exact items.

Contamination has a half-life: benchmark inflation from leaked items decays as training continues on clean data, so where contamination sits in the data stream determines how much of it survives to release.

Memorization capacity per parameter is measurable for vision encoders via graded canary injection, and the bits-per-parameter constant predicts how much verbatim content any release of a given size can carry.

Contamination persistence through fine-tuning depends on the similarity channel: pixel-level leaked content washes out during clean fine-tuning while semantic-level leakage persists, inverting which contamination type matters for released task models.

Text-side contamination inflates zero-shot vision scores without any image overlap: benchmark class vocabularies and item descriptions in alt-text teach the label space, a channel invisible to image-based decontamination.

Contamination is a free rider in fitted scaling laws: as web corpora grow they accumulate more benchmark-adjacent content, so part of every published data-scaling exponent is contamination growth, and decontaminated exponents are measurably smaller.

An inverse-scaling suite for vision: a curated battery of tasks where accuracy reliably decreases with model and data scale (prior-dominance failures), establishing that vision scaling has systematic losers, not just diminishing returns.

U-shaped scaling exists in vision and its trough is movable by data: tasks where a shortcut is learned before the true feature show worse-then-better scale curves, and enriching disambiguating data shifts the trough to smaller scale.

A hard resolution floor breaks data scaling: when the discriminative evidence for a class falls below the token sampling grid, the data-scaling exponent for that class collapses to near zero, and no corpus size compensates.

Tail exhaustion bends the data-scaling curve: growing a crawl under a fixed collection policy yields diminishing unique-information rates, and the bend point is predictable from the crawl's own duplicate-rate trajectory.

The loss-to-capability exchange rate is nonstationary: equal increments of upstream loss improvement buy shrinking downstream gains as scale grows, so upstream-loss-based planning systematically overpromises at the frontier.

Aggregate scaling laws over-promise for rare slices: per-slice exponents are strongly heterogeneous, aggregate fits are dominated by head slices, and tail-slice performance is systematically over-predicted by the global law.

Scaling breaks are data-determined, not architecture-determined: the data scale at which scaling curves bend is shared across architecture families trained on the same corpus, identifying breaks as corpus properties.

More data can hurt minorities of the distribution: at fixed mixture, growing total data amplifies majority-domain dominance and can reduce absolute accuracy on minority domains, a non-monotonicity fixable by share re-weighting, not by more data.

Underwater detectors implicitly regress object range from wavelength-dependent color loss, so swapping the water's optical type at test time moves detections in a direction predictable from attenuation physics.

Per-pixel range-conditioned color correction (inverting attenuation along estimated optical path length) beats global white balance for underwater color fidelity because the illuminant shift varies with distance inside a single image.

In vehicle-lit deep-sea imagery, inverse-square lighting falloff makes image brightness a range proxy, and detectors trained on such data acquire a brightness-centrality prior that flattening the illumination field measurably disrupts.

Marine-snow false positives are separable by their near-camera optical signature (large defocus, high frame-to-frame parallax), so a two-frame defocus-parallax gate removes them without retraining the detector.

Flat-port refraction breaks the pinhole model underwater, so air-trained monocular depth models should exhibit a specific radially increasing depth bias underwater that a Snell-law correction largely removes.

Sunlight caustics dominate temporal gradients in shallow-water video, so trackers follow caustic flicker instead of animals; suppressing the caustic frequency band restores track stability without touching appearance models.

Classification accuracy on marine imagery declines with optical path length according to a spectral-information law reproducible by synthetic re-attenuation, establishing water column optics (not habitat covariates) as the causal driver.

Underwater scenes lack the gravity-aligned ground plane priors of terrestrial imagery, so underwater-trained models should be measurably more rotation-tolerant, and terrestrial models should lose disproportionate accuracy underwater when images are rolled.

Biofouling on fixed underwater observatory cameras is a monotonic, physically irreversible drift, so drift detectors that exploit monotonicity flag fouling substantially earlier than exchangeability-based drift detection.

Surge-induced oscillatory camera and scene motion in shallow benthic video is narrowband and separable in the frequency domain, and removing it improves benthic change detection more than generic video stabilization.

Acoustic shadows in side-scan sonar geometrically encode proud-object height, and a detector head that explicitly regresses height from shadow extent generalizes to unseen target types better than intensity-only detection.

Optical-pretrained backbones carry a light-from-above shading prior that is physically wrong for sonar, so transfer performance should depend on the orientation of the range axis, and a range-axis flip should hurt more than a cross-track flip.

Sonar speckle is multiplicative with Rayleigh-family statistics, so augmentation and consistency training built on multiplicative noise should beat additive-Gaussian recipes imported from optical vision.

Sonar target signatures are so aspect-dependent that single-view recognition has a hard ceiling, and accuracy versus number of fused aspect views should follow a saturating information-accrual curve whose shape identifies the viewing-angle information content.

Multipath ghosts in confined-water sonar occur at geometrically predictable offsets (surface/wall mirror images), so a geometry-conditioned deghosting filter can remove them and cut false positives without suppressing true nearby targets.

Time-varying gain compensation residue leaves range-correlated intensity gradients in sonar images that models exploit as a positional prior, and randomizing gain profiles in training removes a measurable cross-platform transfer penalty.

Cross-frequency sonar transfer is mostly a point-spread-function mismatch: matching resolution via physically derived PSF resampling recovers the bulk of the accuracy lost when models move between sonar frequencies.

Sonar detection difficulty is governed by the ratio of seabed ripple wavelength to target size, peaking near ratio one, giving a predictive environmental-difficulty law rather than a vague 'cluttered seabed' excuse.

Synthetic aperture sonar micronavigation errors leave a characteristic azimuthal smearing signature from which the platform motion error is regressable, enabling learned autofocus that corrects imagery without inertial ground truth.
Predicting the acoustic shadow field from the highlight field is a physics-grounded self-supervised pretext for sonar encoders that beats generic contrastive pretraining in the low-label regime.

Defocus blur in single-plane brightfield microscopy carries recoverable axial (z) information, so a model can output a coarse depth map of subcellular structures from one 2D image, validated against real z-stacks.

Uncorrected illumination inhomogeneity encodes well position in high-content screens, and models exploit it as a shortcut; retrospective flat-field correction measurably changes cross-plate mechanism-of-action generalization.

Photobleaching makes fluorescence intensity a clock, so live-cell models silently conflate biological dynamics with cumulative light exposure; a bleaching-decay invariance test separates the two and most current models fail it.

Spectral bleed-through between fluorescence channels inflates in-silico labeling benchmarks: part of the reported ability to predict one stain from another is optics leakage, quantifiable by evaluating before and after linear unmixing.

Microscopy models are blind to physical scale because micrometers-per-pixel is stripped at training time; injecting physical pixel size as a conditioning token improves cross-magnification and cross-instrument generalization beyond scale augmentation.

Volume electron microscopy is physically anisotropic (section thickness >> lateral pixel size), and 3D models with anisotropy-matched receptive fields should beat isotropic-resampling pipelines on connectomic structures elongated along z.

Batch effects in Cell Painting concentrate in a low-rank optical subspace (illumination, stain intensity, focus), so projecting that subspace out of frozen features recovers cross-batch biology retrieval without any adversarial training.

A PSF-convolved null model provides the missing significance test for learned colocalization claims in fluorescence microscopy: a measurable share of reported subcellular colocalization is reproducible by optics alone.

Cell division breaks the augmentation-invariance assumption of contrastive learning, and a mitosis-aware pretext that treats division as identity-split (one-to-two positives) yields better cell-state representations than standard temporal contrastive pretraining.
Phase-contrast halos are signed optical artifacts that encode local optical-thickness gradients, so a network can invert halos into a quantitative-phase proxy map from ordinary phase-contrast images.

Stain augmentation performed in optical-density space (where Beer-Lambert absorption is linear) transfers across scanners better than RGB-space color jitter at equal augmentation diversity, because it respects the physics of stain mixing.

WSI pyramids are stored with lossy JPEG whose 8x8 block artifacts interact with cell-scale texture, and pathology models measurably encode scanner-compression fingerprints, contaminating cross-site evaluations.

Pathology foundation models trained on single-magnification tiles have weak cross-magnification feature consistency, and enforcing pyramid-consistency at pretraining measurably improves slide-level diagnosis that depends on multi-scale context.

Spatial statistics of cell-neighborhood composition (tissue-graph features) carry outcome signal beyond tile-appearance MIL, testable by whether a graph head on cell centroids improves survival prediction over appearance-only aggregation.

Archival stain fading makes slide age a decodable covariate in retrospective pathology cohorts, and age-confounded splits inflate reported prognostic performance because outcome follow-up length correlates with slide age.

DAB chromogen deposition in immunohistochemistry is optically nonlinear and non-stoichiometric, so end-to-end learned IHC scorers inherit a saturation bias that a physics-corrected optical-density front end measurably reduces.

Scanner-to-scanner color shift in pathology is a low-dimensional physical transform (illuminant plus sensor response), estimable from unlabeled tiles without correspondence, and applying the estimated transform recovers most cross-scanner accuracy without retraining.

Attention maps from slide-level MIL models are routinely presented as lesion localization, but on small lesions their localization accuracy may be near chance even when slide-level AUC is high, because MIL can classify from field effects.

Regressing molecular tumor purity from H&E morphology and mapping where the regression fails identifies which molecular properties are morphologically visible, giving a principled boundary for 'omics-from-slides' claims.

Predictions from WSI models are inconsistent across pyramid levels of the same slide, and enforcing cross-level agreement at inference (a free ensemble over the pyramid) improves robustness to scanner sharpness differences.

OCR and handwriting models increasingly read from language priors instead of pixels as degradation grows, measurable by a matched pseudoword substitution test whose accuracy gap quantifies hallucination risk.

Bleed-through in double-sided historical documents is a mirrored, blurred copy of the verso page, so jointly modeling recto and verso scans inverts it physically and beats single-side restoration for downstream recognition.

Binarization, still the first step of many document pipelines, destroys stroke-interior and grayscale evidence that end-to-end recognizers exploit, and the information loss can be quantified as a degradation-dependent CER penalty law.

Reading order is the invisible output dimension of document AI: systems with identical detection scores can scramble token order enough to corrupt downstream LLM consumption, and an order-sensitive metric exposes large hidden quality differences.

Static handwriting is the trace of a motor process, and pretraining recognizers to recover stroke dynamics (order, direction, velocity) from online-handwriting-derived pairs improves offline recognition of cursive where letter segmentation is ambiguous.

Table understanding fails structurally on merged and nested cells because decoders emit token sequences without grid-consistency constraints; grammar-constrained decoding eliminates a specific, countable class of structural errors.

A page is internally consistent in hand and typeface, so per-page unsupervised adaptation (estimating one style code per page and conditioning the decoder) should beat both global models and per-glyph adaptation on historical text.

Chart-understanding models rely on rendering-template priors rather than measuring geometry: re-rendering identical data with unusual axis scales and styles collapses extraction accuracy in a way that quantifies template reliance versus true visual measurement.

Repeated photocopying acts as an iterated contraction on glyph shapes with predictable attractors, so augmenting OCR training with physically iterated copy-degradation beats single-pass noise models for multi-generation documents.

Whitespace is a first-class structural object in documents (gutters, margins, indentation carry the layout grammar), and representing detected whitespace separators as explicit tokens improves layout parsing of complex pages over ink-only detection.

Form key-value binding follows a small set of spatial grammars (label left, label above, boxed pairs), and models fail predictably when a form's grammar differs from the training majority; grammar-conditioned binding closes most of the gap.

The born-digital-to-scan gap in document AI decomposes into measurable physical factors (geometric warp, sensor noise, illumination), and factor-wise ablation will show geometric warp dominates, redirecting augmentation effort.

Cross-page structure (running headers, footers, continued articles) is trivially identifiable by inter-page matching yet routinely misparsed by single-page models; a cross-page voting layer eliminates a whole error class in book and report parsing.

Camera-captured page curl is a developable surface (zero Gaussian curvature), and dewarping models constrained to developable solutions should beat free-form flow fields on downstream OCR, especially off the training distribution.

Mathematical notation is a 2D grammar whose errors are invisible to string metrics: models with equal token accuracy differ hugely in structural correctness, and tree-constrained decoding for math recovers a measurable share of semantic fidelity.

SAR layover and shadow are deterministic functions of incidence angle and terrain, so feeding the per-pixel local incidence angle as an input channel improves SAR building extraction more than any equivalent amount of extra training imagery.

Physically derived polarimetric features (channel ratios and decompositions) add label-efficiency to SAR land-cover models: their advantage over raw dual-pol channels is largest at low label budgets and vanishes with abundant labels, quantifying what the physics is worth.

Same-tile multi-temporal imagery isolates the sun-geometry shortcut in optical remote sensing: land-cover predictions flip with sun elevation on unchanged scenes, quantifying a shadow-driven confound that scene-level models silently exploit.

Off-nadir viewing angle degrades building extraction through two separable mechanisms (facade visibility and resolution anisotropy), and an angle-conditioned model that reasons about facade displacement beats angle-agnostic training on high-off-nadir imagery.

Models trained on top-of-atmosphere reflectance partially learn the atmosphere: paired L1C/L2A evaluation of the same scenes will show atmospherically corrected training transfers better across dates and regions by a measurable margin.

Terrain shadow is computable from public elevation models and sun ephemeris, so DEM-informed illumination correction should recover mountain land-cover accuracy that learned models lose, quantifying how much 'hard terrain' error is deterministic optics.

Band-dropout training makes multispectral models band-set-invariant, enabling zero-shot transfer across sensors with different band configurations (Sentinel-2 to Landsat) at a small, quantified cost on the native sensor.

Pan-sharpening hallucinates high-frequency chroma that shifts small-object detection in measurable ways, so detection pipelines consuming pan-sharpened products inherit fabrication errors invisible in image-quality metrics.

Optical biomass and canopy-height regressors hide a physical saturation ceiling: stratifying error by lidar-measured structure will show accuracy collapses beyond the spectral saturation point while global metrics look healthy, and SAR fusion lifts specifically that stratum.

Re-indexing crop time series by accumulated growing-degree-days instead of calendar time aligns phenology across years and regions, and temporal models re-parameterized this way transfer across seasons with measurably less degradation.

A seasonal-null baseline (predicting this-season appearance from historical same-season imagery) reveals how much of 'change detection' performance is actually season recognition, recalibrating a benchmark-heavy subfield.

Urbanization is nearly irreversible at monitoring timescales, and decoding land-cover time series under a monotonicity constraint removes temporal flicker while leaving accuracy unchanged, exploiting process physics that frame-independent models ignore.

Sensor-generation transitions in long satellite archives masquerade as environmental change: a measurable excess of detected 'changes' coincides with instrument switchovers, biasing multi-decade trend analyses built on learned models.

Thermal inertia is a material fingerprint: conditioning land-surface-temperature models on acquisition time-of-day and exploiting day-night temperature phase separates materials that single-snapshot spectral models confuse.

Gap-filled satellite composites systematically underestimate change rates because interpolation hallucinates stability; the bias is measurable by masking clear time series and comparing recovered versus true change statistics.

Ship wakes in SAR encode vessel speed and heading through Kelvin-wake geometry, so a detector with a wake-regression head produces velocity estimates for free, verifiable at scale against transponder tracks.

Geospatial temporal encoders built on calendar features fail hemisphere transfer because seasons flip; encoding time by local phenological phase instead of date enables north-south transfer at a measurable fraction of within-hemisphere accuracy.

Logical anomalies (missing/misplaced components) defeat patch-statistics anomaly detectors by construction, and the failure is predictable from a detector's receptive-field statistics, separating the field's methods into two non-competing classes.

Industrial anomaly benchmarks are near-perfectly registered, and injecting realistic fixture jitter (small pose/scale perturbations) collapses leaderboard methods at rates that reveal how much reported performance is registration rather than representation.

Surface defect visibility is BRDF-gated: many scratches and dents are invisible under any single illumination but detectable in multi-illumination stacks, and the invisible fraction is measurable, bounding what single-image inspection can ever achieve.

Defect mechanism, not product identity, is the right unit of generalization in industrial inspection: models transfer better across products within the same defect physics (scratch, dent, contamination) than across defect types on the same product.

Beam-hardening artifacts in industrial X-ray CT mimic porosity defects at geometry-predictable locations, and injecting a physics-computed artifact map as an input channel cuts false calls in casting inspection without any new labels.

Active thermography sequences contain subsurface defect signatures in their temporal decay curves that no single frame carries, and spatiotemporal models on thermal transients should beat frame-based models by a margin that quantifies the temporal information content.

Monocular depth underwater is not scale-ambiguous the way it is in air: wavelength-dependent attenuation provides an absolute range cue, so a lightweight attenuation-reading head can convert relative depth maps into metric depth without stereo or sonar.

Underwater place recognition fails across long-term revisits mainly because the water changed, not the scene: a per-survey physics-estimated attenuation normalization applied before descriptor extraction restores cross-survey retrieval without any retraining.

Species discrimination from fisheries echosounder data improves with added acoustic frequencies according to a saturating law whose per-species-pair knee is predicted by swim-bladder resonance physics, not by generic more-channels-help arguments.

Wreck and boulder detectors on multibeam bathymetry silently overfit the arbitrary hillshade rendering azimuth, missing targets whose long axis aligns with the artificial light; multi-azimuth rendering or gradient-native inputs make detection azimuth-invariant.

Under a shrinking photon budget, microscopy classes fail in an order predicted by the spatial scale and contrast of their diagnostic features (a Rose-criterion ordering), making low-dose robustness a per-class physical quantity rather than a model property.

3D microscopy segmentation benchmarks are quietly dominated by shallow, aberration-free planes: refractive-index mismatch degrades the PSF with imaging depth, and depth-stratified scoring plus PSF-matched augmentation exposes and partially closes a gap that headline numbers hide.

Learned single-molecule localization networks hit a breakdown emitter density set by PSF-overlap statistics: the breakdown point scales predictably with PSF width and barely moves with more training data — an optics-set capability ceiling.

Tissue folds have an exact physical signature that no other artifact shares — near-doubled optical density in both stain channels with an unchanged stain ratio — so a label-free stain-physics fold detector can inoculate slide-level models against a dominant failure mode.

TCGA's paired frozen and FFPE slides of the same tumors are an untapped natural experiment: the frozen-section gap is a task-structured quantity — largest for nuclear-texture-dependent predictions — and predictable per case from an ice-artifact severity score.

Newsprint halftone screens are periodic and FFT-detectable, so per-page physics-based descreening — notching the measured screen frequency before recognition — beats generic learned denoising for OCR on scanned newspapers at near-zero compute.

OCR breakdown under low resolution is governed by x-height in pixels, not DPI, font, or model: character-error curves from different documents and recognizers collapse onto one sampling-limited master curve with a knee near the stroke Nyquist limit.

Document VQA models often answer forms from layout-template priors instead of reading: swapping a field's printed value in place (font-matched, pixel-consistent) leaves a measurable fraction of answers stuck at the old value, concentrated on frequent templates.

Professionally typeset pages sit on a hidden baseline grid; estimating the grid from projection-profile autocorrelation and snapping line hypotheses to it removes the merge/split errors that dominate dense-layout parsing, with no learning required.

Cross-dataset transfer in layout analysis is predicted by a computable layout-grammar distance (region-type transition and geometry statistics), not by visual similarity: transfer drops fall on one curve against grammar distance across dataset pairs.

Born-digital PDFs carry exact vector primitives (rules, paths, glyph boxes) that pixel-based table models throw away by re-rasterizing; a primitive-aware input stream recovers borderless and hairline-ruled structure that no practical raster resolution restores.

Homogeneous industrial surfaces are stationary random textures, so spectral whitening — flattening the normal class's estimated power spectrum — is the physically matched preprocessing for texture anomaly detection, lifting patch-based detectors selectively on texture categories.

How hard a product is for one-class anomaly detection is a measurable property of its normal-appearance manifold: intrinsic dimensionality of nominal patch embeddings predicts per-category AUROC across detector families, quoting inspection difficulty before any defect is seen.

Industrial anomaly benchmarks' nominal training sets are near-duplicates from fixed fixtures: effective nominal diversity is tiny, so few-shot and coreset-memory results largely restate dataset redundancy rather than method quality.

Speckle is temporally uncorrelated while the scene persists, so temporal multilooking of Sentinel-1 stacks is the physically matched denoiser for SAR crop classification — beating stronger spatial despeckling at equal compute and following the predicted inverse-square-root variance law.

Tide height at acquisition time is exactly computable from harmonic models, yet coastal change detection treats intertidal exposure as scene change; tide-stage-aware pairing or conditioning removes a dominant class of false coastal 'changes' at zero labeling cost.

UAV crop-monitoring orthomosaics carry a BRDF hotspot artifact: view-sun geometry varies across flight lines, imprinting periodic stripes into model predictions that follow solar geometry rather than the field — a quantifiable, correctable bias in precision-agriculture maps.

Cross-site failure in wheat-head detection is substantially a physical sampling mismatch: deterministic ground-sample-distance standardization closes a large share of the domain gap that heavy scale augmentation fails to close, and the residual correlates with non-scale factors.

A paired same-image comparison protocol for detectors, using per-image score differences with sign-flip permutation tests, shrinks comparison uncertainty enough to change published accept/reject conclusions at fixed test-set size.

A reference-decoder evaluation contract that pins score thresholds, NMS behavior, and max-detections into a single frozen decoding specification makes detector rankings invariant across evaluation harnesses.

Error-decomposition-matched interventions: choosing the training fix whose target matches the dominant TIDE-style error type of a detector yields reliably larger gains than a mismatched fix, making error decomposition an actionable prescription rather than a diagnostic.

A minimum-detectable-difference (MDD) certificate for detection benchmarks, computed from hierarchical resampling over images and seeds, lets leaderboards refuse deltas below the resolvable threshold and changes which published improvements count as real.

An assignment-cost metric that scores detectors by optimal bipartite matching between predicted and ground-truth sets, replacing threshold-and-NMS-dependent AP, removes the max-detections confound and re-ranks end-to-end versus NMS-based detectors.

Item-response-theory benchmark compression: modeling images as items with difficulty/discrimination and detectors as abilities enables an adaptive 1k-image COCO subset that reproduces full-benchmark rankings at 5x lower evaluation cost.

Automatic consensus completion of missing test-set annotations by heterogeneous-detector agreement reproduces most conclusion changes obtained by expensive human relabeling, turning test-set repair into a zero-annotation capability.

Occlusion-stratified, deployment-weighted detection scoring: reporting AP within occlusion strata and reweighting to a declared deployment occlusion distribution changes model selection relative to uniform COCO AP.

A human-anchored composite detection metric, fitted on a small set of expert pairwise preferences between model outputs, predicts held-out human judgments substantially better than AP and can be shipped as a frozen scoring function.

Verifier-completed federated evaluation: converting LVIS-style federated AP into an estimate of complete AP by running a high-precision presence verifier over unlabeled categories changes rare-class conclusions.

A seed-versus-data compute-allocation rule for trustworthy detector comparisons: given a fixed GPU budget, splitting compute across 3 short-seed replicates beats one long run for deciding between two training recipes.

A frozen-backbone comparison track for detection heads: evaluating head designs on a shared frozen public backbone reproduces full-finetuning rank order at an order of magnitude less compute, enabling cheap pre-screening of architectural claims.

Convention-conditioned segmentation: a single model trained with a dataset-convention token on images annotated under two mask conventions matches per-convention specialists and enables continuous convention control at inference.

Rater-conditioned decoding for multi-annotator segmentation: conditioning on an annotator embedding reproduces individual raters' styles and transfers to unseen raters from 5 examples, outperforming consensus-trained models on every rater.

Two-pass precision-tiered annotation: labeling most of a dataset coarsely and a small fraction precisely, with a tolerance-weighted loss that knows which pixels are trustworthy, reaches near-full-precision performance at roughly half the annotation cost.

Divergence-routed relabeling: routing only the instances where architecturally diverse models disagree to human relabeling recovers most of the benefit of relabeling an entire benchmark at a small fraction of the cost, validated against a public full re-annotation.

Format-native mixed-supervision training: consuming polygons, raw pixel masks, and boxes through format-specific losses (instead of converting everything to one format) yields a measurable gain when merging heterogeneous datasets.

Convention-marginalized training: augmenting ground-truth masks with rule-based convention transforms (dilation, erosion, hole policy, part-inclusion toggles) during training produces models that transfer across datasets with different annotation standards.

Rosetta-subset taxonomy bridging: a small dual-labeled image subset shared between two datasets suffices to learn an empirical label-space mapping that beats name-based taxonomy alignment for training merged-vocabulary models.

Set-valued ground truth evaluation: scoring predictions against the set of plausible annotations (from multi-rater data) with best-match credit changes model rankings relative to consensus-mask scoring.

Annotation-time geometric verification: a verifier model that flags boundary-inconsistent masks during labeling catches a majority of the errors that later required a full public re-annotation to fix, at a low false-flag rate.

Certified-negative annotation: spending a small budget on explicitly verified empty regions (rather than more positives) recovers a large share of the performance lost to federated/missing-label training.
Complexity-indexed precision budgeting: allocating polygon vertex budgets by boundary complexity (not uniformly) cuts total annotation clicks by a third at equal downstream segmentation quality.

Output-space convention adapters: a small morphological-plus-learned operator fitted on 50 dual-convention examples translates a trained model's masks between annotation standards at evaluation time, recovering most of the convention-induced score gap without retraining.

Anchored benchmark refresh: shipping every benchmark version with difficulty-anchor items shared across versions yields a contamination certificate — models whose refreshed-set drop exceeds the anchor-predicted drop are flagged, changing conclusions about claimed progress.

Hierarchical variance power-tables for segmentation benchmarks: decomposing score variance into image, class, and seed components lets a benchmark publish per-delta statistical power, and applying power-gated acceptance changes a third of small claimed improvements.

Sequential evaluation with early stopping: a sequential probability ratio test over streaming per-image comparisons reaches the same accept/reject decisions as full-test evaluation using a fraction of the images, enabling cheap continuous model monitoring.

Battery-level acceptance testing: requiring claimed improvements to survive a hierarchical test across a fixed battery of related benchmarks (instead of one headline dataset) changes which methods count as improvements, and the battery can be assembled entirely from public sets.

Frozen reference-harness containers for dense-prediction scoring: pinning the entire evaluation stack in a versioned container eliminates the score drift that library upgrades silently introduce, making cross-year comparisons valid.

Declared-prior evaluation: benchmarks accept a user-declared deployment prior over strata (scene type, object scale, occlusion) and return reweighted scores with variance guarantees, replacing ad-hoc subset evaluations with a supported query interface.

Pre-registered tradeoff-cone acceptance: replacing single-scalar improvement tests with a Pareto-dominance test over a declared metric cone (region overlap plus boundary quality) reverses accepted wins that traded one competence for another.

Cryptographic canary items for vision benchmarks: seeding test sets with arbitrary-labeled canary images gives benchmark hosts a statistically powered detector of training-on-test contamination that works as a protocol, not a forensic investigation.

Noise-ceiling-normalized leaderboards: estimating each benchmark's inter-annotator ceiling and reporting scores as fractions of remaining headroom changes which improvements look meaningful, especially near saturation.

Difficulty-matched test refresh: replacing stale test images with fresh ones matched on anchor-model difficulty profiles preserves model rankings while breaking URL-level and hash-level contamination, enabling routine benchmark rotation.

Partial-pooling estimators for rare-class metrics: hierarchical shrinkage of per-class AP/IoU stabilizes long-tail leaderboards, halving bootstrap rank volatility and changing which long-tail methods win.

Boundary-affinity point supervision: growing instance masks from a 10-click-per-image budget through an affinity field trained only on click pairs reaches most of full-mask panoptic quality, because clicks constrain topology while affinities carry geometry.

Box-plus-one-interior-point supervision: adding a single interior click to each box annotation closes more than half of the box-only-to-full-mask instance segmentation gap by resolving the figure-ground ambiguity that box supervision cannot.

Scribble supervision with a topology-preserving connectivity loss recovers thin-structure segmentation (poles, fences, sign posts) that standard scribble training loses, at unchanged cost on thick classes.

SSL-native weak supervision: replacing CAM-style seeds with clustering of frozen self-supervised features as the seed generator lifts image-label-only segmentation by a measurable margin under an otherwise identical pipeline.

Complement-masked training for disjointly labeled dataset unions: masking the loss over classes a source did not label, plus cross-image class banks, trains one model from three partially labeled datasets to near fully-labeled-union quality.

A clicks-to-quality scaling law: interactive annotation quality follows a power law in click budget whose exponent is shared across datasets and interfaces, enabling annotation-budget planning from a 50-image pilot.

Train-time depth as free boundary supervision: distilling depth-discontinuity and normal-discontinuity maps from RGB-D training data into a 2D segmentation model improves boundary quality with zero test-time depth requirement.

One-exemplar dataset bootstrapping: a single annotated exemplar per class, propagated through frozen-feature retrieval and geometric verification, generates pseudo-labels sufficient to train a segmentation model to a large fraction of full supervision.

Verified negatives are the high-value half of weak supervision: human-verified negative image-level labels (already shipped in Open Images) improve weakly supervised detection more per label than an equal number of extra positives.

Budget-optimal supervision mixing: a cost-model-driven allocator that chooses per-image supervision grade (clicks, boxes, or masks) from image statistics beats any single-grade budget spend on final model quality.

Occlusion-order supervision is sufficient for amodal completion: training with only pairwise over/under relations (free from existing overlap annotations) yields amodal masks competitive with fully amodal-supervised training.

Amodal-extent anchor assignment: assigning training targets by estimated full-object extent instead of visible-box overlap recovers detections of heavily occluded objects that visible-IoU assignment systematically starves of positive anchors.

T-junction-based occlusion ordering without order labels: a local junction-geometry classifier recovers pairwise over/under relations at high accuracy, supplying free ordering supervision for amodal pipelines.

Occlusion-graded curriculum by real-segment compositing: pasting real instance segments with progressively increasing overlap teaches occlusion robustness that random-paste augmentation misses, at identical augmentation budget.

Amodal-overlap duplicate reasoning: replacing visible-IoU NMS with suppression decisions based on estimated amodal overlap preserves detections of objects hidden behind others, recovering recall that visible-box suppression destroys.

Context-driven proposal of fully hidden objects: a detector head trained on synthetic full-occlusion composites learns to propose completely invisible objects from scene context at usable precision, a capability absent from every current detector.

Category-agnostic amodal completion: an amodal head trained on one category family transfers most of its occlusion-completion skill to unseen categories, showing amodal reasoning is shape-generic and can ship as a universal module.

Layered panoptic decoding: representing the scene as depth-ordered mask layers instead of a flat label map fixes boundary-ownership errors between overlapping instances, improving contested-boundary accuracy at equal overall quality.

Backbone-portable feature upsamplers: a high-resolution feature upsampler trained once on one frozen backbone transfers to other backbones with most of its dense-task benefit intact, so upsampling can ship as a universal plug-in rather than a per-model accessory.

Implicit coordinate-based dense readout beats deconvolutional heads at matched compute on boundary accuracy, because continuous decoding removes the grid-aliasing that upsampling stacks bake into predictions.

A standardized dense-probe suite (multi-task, nonlinear-local, resolution-swept) for frozen backbones produces backbone rankings that differ from linear-probe rankings and better reflect finetuned downstream ordering.

Frequency-matched layer selection: choosing which backbone layers to fuse for a dense task by matching layer frequency response to the task's spatial-frequency demand replaces exhaustive layer search at a tenth of the cost.

Anti-aliased patch embedding: replacing the ViT patchify stem with an anti-aliased convolutional downsampler measurably improves thin-structure segmentation at equal compute, because patchify aliases exactly the high-frequency content thin classes live in.

Retrofit register tokens for dense readout: adding register tokens during a short continued-pretraining phase cleans the high-norm artifact tokens of existing ViT checkpoints and improves frozen-feature dense probes without full re-pretraining.

Cross-backbone feature translators: a light translator network mapping one frozen backbone's feature space into another's lets task heads trained on the target backbone run on the source backbone, enabling a head-reuse marketplace across the model zoo.

Resolution-extrapolation recipes for dense inference: a position-encoding rescaling law plus attention-temperature correction lets models trained at 512px infer at 2048px with minimal degradation, unlocking high-resolution deployment without high-resolution training.

Task-vector merging works for dense heads when decoder families match: merging detection and segmentation specialists finetuned from one base yields a single model near both specialists, with decoder-family compatibility as the governing condition.

Annotation-convention directions in weight space: interpolating between checkpoints finetuned on two mask conventions traces a monotone boundary-style continuum, giving deployment-time convention control from a single stored direction vector.

Dense-task finetuning edits are layer-sparse: most of a task vector's effect concentrates in a small fraction of layers, so sparse task-delta storage and merging preserve capability at a fifth of the memory and interference cost.

Pre-merge orthogonalization: projecting task vectors to reduce their pairwise conflict before merging recovers a large share of the performance lost to interference, turning merge quality from a lottery into a controlled procedure.

Permutation-aligned merging of independently trained dense models: re-basin alignment extends from classifiers to segmentation networks, enabling federated-style averaging of models trained by different parties without shared initialization.

Vocabulary-union merging: two detectors finetuned from one base on disjoint category sets merge into a single model detecting the union within a small gap of joint training, eliminating the need to pool datasets for vocabulary growth.

A merge-compatibility rule for the dense-model zoo: mergeability is gated by assignment-mechanism identity (Hungarian-matching vs dense-assignment decoders), a checkable property that predicts merge success better than architecture names or task labels.

Containment-projected part-whole decoding: enforcing part-inside-whole as a hard projection layer at decoding time eliminates containment violations and improves part segmentation without hurting whole-object quality.

Relational-consistency re-decoding for detection: an energy-based pass that rescoring detections against learned object-relation statistics (support, co-occurrence, relative scale) recovers context-inconsistent misses and suppresses relation-violating false positives.

Connectivity-constrained lane decoding: decoding lane markings as connected curve sets with a hard continuity constraint halves broken-lane errors at equal pixel accuracy, because breakage is an output-space artifact rather than a perception failure.

Hierarchy-consistent decoding for classification: constraining predictions to respect the WordNet hierarchy at decode time reduces severe mistakes substantially at equal top-1, delivering the mistake-severity benefit of hierarchical training without retraining.

Learned exclusion-composition matrices for panoptic decoding: a soft constraint matrix over class pairs (mutual exclusion, adjacency plausibility) applied during mask assembly reduces stuff-thing confusion errors at equal PQ elsewhere.

Reflection-equivariant heads for man-made categories: enforcing horizontal-mirror equivariance in the decoder improves boundary quality on bilaterally symmetric classes without degrading asymmetric ones, isolating symmetry as an exploitable output prior.

Kinematic-manifold projection for 2D pose: projecting keypoint predictions onto a learned manifold of anthropometrically valid poses at decode time eliminates impossible outputs and improves occluded-joint accuracy on frozen pose models.

Context-matched rare-class transplantation: pasting rare-class instances into co-occurrence-plausible scenes (instead of random images) drives significantly larger rare-class gains, showing context plausibility is an active ingredient of paste augmentation for the tail.

Shape-prototype sharing for the tail: letting rare classes inherit mask-decoding prototypes from shape-similar frequent classes improves rare mask quality without hurting the head, because mask geometry transfers across semantic boundaries.

Verified-negative-filtered retrieval harvesting for tail classes: mining extra rare-class training crops from Open Images with verification filtering yields large tail gains, and the filtering step, not the volume, carries most of the benefit.

Prototype attachment for novel classes: attaching a feature-prototype classifier head for a new class to a frozen detector reaches a usable fraction of full-finetuning AP from 10 examples with provably zero base-class regression.

Superclass-fallback decoding for the tail: predicting the most specific taxonomy node whose evidence clears a rank-based support rule turns unreliable rare-class guesses into reliable coarser labels, reducing severe errors at fixed specificity budgets.

Visual-exemplar anchors beat name anchors for the tail: defining rare categories by a handful of exemplar embeddings instead of class-name text improves tail detection, because rare-class names are exactly where text grounding is weakest.

Decoupled localize-then-specialize decoding for fine-grained tails: localizing at a coarse reliable level and classifying crops with a dedicated fine-grained head beats end-to-end fine-grained detection when leaf classes are rare, quantifying a frequency threshold for decoupling.

Correction propagation across a dataset: one human fix to a model error, matched through frozen-feature similarity, automatically repairs the same error mode across thousands of images with bounded collateral damage.

Learned click policies for interactive segmentation: a policy trained to choose the next click location (rather than the fixed largest-error-center heuristic) reduces clicks-to-target-quality by a quarter across datasets and models.

Exclusion prompts as a first-class interaction type: adding not-this clicks that carve away distractor regions cuts interaction budgets on cluttered scenes beyond what additional positive clicks achieve.

Batch prompting through correspondence: one prompted image labels a hundred similar images by transporting the prompt through dense correspondences, achieving most of per-image prompting quality at a fraction of the interaction cost.

Optimal single-question disambiguation: when a prompt is ambiguous between part, object, and group, one automatically chosen binary question (is the handle included?) resolves the ambiguity more reliably than an extra click, measured by post-interaction accuracy.

Prompt-once, read-many consistency: a shared prompt encoder that drives segmentation, part, and attribute heads from one prompt produces mutually consistent multi-task outputs, halving cross-head contradiction rates at equal per-task accuracy.

Interaction-noise training for prompt robustness: injecting realistic misclick and imprecision noise into prompt simulation during training halves output variance under real-user-level prompt jitter without degrading clean-prompt accuracy.

Object-adversarial attribute factorization: training the attribute pathway with gradient reversal against object identity yields attribute features that recombine with unseen objects, lifting unseen-composition recognition beyond joint-head baselines.

Translational relation composition: embedding visual relations as vector translations between subject and object features enables zero-shot recognition of unseen subject-relation-object triplets at rates well above joint-classifier baselines.

Region-tokenized pooling preserves feature binding: replacing global pooling with segmentation-guided region tokens fixes the two-object attribute-binding failures of pooled representations, on natural images and without language supervision.

Part-graph recognition for viewpoint compositionality: classifying objects through an explicit part-and-adjacency graph retains accuracy on held-out viewpoints where holistic classifiers collapse, quantifying the structural route to pose generalization.

Exemplar-difference queries: specifying a visual concept by positive minus negative exemplar sets (cups, minus cups-with-handles) defines a retrieval and detection interface that resolves concepts names cannot express, with measurable precision on public data.

Context-swap training for context-robust recognition: replacing backgrounds with segmentation-guided plausible alternatives during training yields classifiers that keep in-context accuracy while gaining strongly on out-of-context objects.

A frozen class-agnostic boundary stream as a universal instance prior: feeding generic boundary-detector features alongside backbone features improves instance segmentation on datasets never seen by either component, because instance separation is boundary-limited out of domain.

Mask-derived box supervision sharpens localization: refitting training boxes from instance masks (which encode extent more precisely than drawn boxes) improves tight-IoU detection metrics with zero new annotation.

Part-segmentation auxiliary supervision for occluded keypoints: jointly training 2D pose with human-part masks improves occluded-joint localization specifically, because part extents carry the evidence that point supervision under occlusion lacks.

Self-supervised attention as an open-world objectness prior: injecting SSL attention-derived objectness into proposal generation recovers novel-class proposals that supervised RPNs suppress, raising open-set recall without hurting known classes.

Stuff-context conditioning for thing detection: conditioning detector queries on stuff-segmentation tokens improves context-dependent object classes, quantifying how much detection has been leaving on the table by ignoring stuff.

Skeleton-seeded part-mask bootstrapping: expanding keypoint skeletons into part pseudo-masks via feature-geodesic propagation trains human part segmentation to a large fraction of fully supervised quality using zero part annotations.
